bai_doc.chu:
Eating healthy is not about strict diets or giving up the foods you love. Instead, it is about feeling great, having more energy, and keeping your body strong. A balanced diet provides your body with the nutrients it needs to function correctly.

Your diet should consist of:
• Half of your plate should consist of fruits and vegetables, which are full of vitamins and fiber.
• One-quarter of your plate should include lean proteins like chicken, fish, beans, or tofu to help build muscle.
• One-quarter of your plate should feature whole grains, such as brown rice or whole-wheat bread, which provide long-lasting energy.

Drinking enough water is another essential part of good nutrition. Sugary drinks, like soda and fruit juices with added sugar, can cause energy crashes and unwanted weight gain. Finally, listening to your body's hunger signals helps you stop eating when you are full, preventing overeating.

**Vocabulary Focus**
**Nutrients:** Substances in food that your body needs to live, grow, and stay healthy.
**Lean protein:** Protein sources that have a low fat content.
**Whole grains:** Grains that retain all parts of the seed (e.g., oats, brown rice, whole wheat).

bai_doc.tieu_de: A Girl Called Owl (Amy Wilson) — Learner’s Book 1.5
bai_doc.tieu_de_html: A Girl Called Owl (Amy Wilson) — Learner’s Book 1.5
bai_doc.chu:
When you have a kid, don’t call it something stupid.
Don’t call it Apple or Pear or Mung Bean.
Don’t call it Owl.
This advice is a bit late for me. Because she did. She did call me Owl. Thirteen years ago she looked down at a tiny little baby – me – and decided that Owl would be a good way to go.
I guess she didn’t know then that I would have white-blond hair that flicks around my face, like feathers, no matter what I do with it. That my eyes would turn from baby blue to the palest brown, almost yellow; that my nose would be on the beaky side.
She should have seen that last one coming though; I inherited it from her.
I like owls. I think they’re beautiful, but you know, my head doesn’t rotate 360 degrees. I can’t fly. I don’t hunt at night.
All these are questions the other kids have asked me, over the years. Mum laughs when I tell her.
‘See!’ she cries, looking up from whatever she’s doing, a glint in her dark eyes. ‘Already you stand out in the crowd. Already you are different. Isn’t it a wonderful thing?’
She’s beautiful, my mum. Not in a subjective way, like she’s my mum therefore she must be beautiful. She’s actually beautiful. She has these big dark eyes, masses of dark hair, and when she smiles, when she laughs, it’s difficult not to join in.
I do try my very best not to join in.
Her name is Isolde. She wears lots of bright colours, and tinkling bangles on her wrists. She smells of warm things: vanilla, cinnamon, oranges and blackcurrants, and something deeper that’s just her, I guess.
My friends love her.
Which is annoying.

Part 2
Owl and her friend, Mallory, have just had a maths lesson. Owl was told off by the teacher for sketching owls instead of paying attention.
It was an owl. The doodle in my maths book. I draw them, over and over. Little ones, big ones, owls with crazy whirly eyes, owls swooping down from the sky. They’re in all the borders of my lined school books. They’re on Post-it notes around my bedroom. I have sketches of them, paintings, even little clay figures.
I’m not saying they’re good. Actually, if you walked into my bedroom, you’d probably run back out again, screaming. They’re a bit intense.
Mum loves them. Loves them. She thinks it’s me expressing myself.
Drawing myself, over and over again.
Mallory just rolls her eyes when she sees a new one now. She bought me a card with a puffin on it for my birthday a couple of weeks ago.
‘Maybe a change?’ she wrote inside, ‘Now that you’re thirteen?’
But I’m not called Puffin.
And there had to be a reason.
A reason Mum called me Owl.

bai_doc.chu:
**Nadine** — I love playing volleyball because it’s easy to learn and great fun! All you need is a volleyball and a net. It’s played by two six-player teams on a court or on the beach. The object is to hit the ball over the net with your hands. The other team have to try to hit it back before it touches the ground. If not, your team wins a point.
**Dani** — I started playing this game two years ago after going to see a tennis championship. It was so exciting to watch, I knew I had to try it! It’s played on a grass or clay court. You can play singles with two players or doubles with four players. You hit a ball with a racquet over a net to your opponent who hits it back. If they miss the ball or it hits the net, your opponent wins a point.

bai_doc.chu:
In December 1891, a gym teacher named James Naismith wanted to find a game his students could play indoors during the cold winters in Massachusetts. He nailed two peach baskets to the balcony railings of the gym and used a soccer ball for the game. Unlike today, the baskets had solid bottoms, so every time a player scored, the referee had to climb a ladder to get the ball back!
As the game grew, people made changes to make it faster and more exciting. In the beginning, there were no backboards, which meant fans in the balcony could reach over and block the shots. Backboards were added to stop this from happening. The soccer ball was eventually replaced by a larger orange ball that was easier to bounce and grip.
In 1946, the Basketball Association of America was formed, which later became the National Basketball Association (NBA) in 1949. This organization helped turn basketball into a professional sport. Today, players like LeBron James and Michael Jordan are famous for their skills, but it all began with a soccer ball and two peach baskets.

bai_doc.chu:
Maya is an eleven-year-old swimmer who trains at the National Junior Sports Academy. Every morning, Maya wakes up at 5:30 a.m. to prepare for her first training session. Being an elite athlete requires intense dedication, hard work, and strict discipline.
"If you want to reach the finals, you must practice every day," explains Coach Harrison. "If a swimmer skips training without a valid reason, they will lose their endurance very quickly."
At the academy, young athletes learn that success is not just about winning medals; it is also about staying healthy and respecting the rules of sportsmanship. Athletes need to follow a balanced diet rich in carbohydrates and protein. They ought to sleep at least nine hours every night so their muscles can recover properly. Coach Harrison always reminds his team: "You shouldn't eat junk food before a big race, and you mustn't forget to stretch your muscles before entering the pool. Skipping your warmup can cause severe muscle injuries."
However, training isn't always intense. On Sundays, Maya needn't wake up early because it is her official rest day. "Rest is just as important as hard work," Maya says. "If I take time to rest on Sunday, I will feel energized and ready for Monday's workouts."
Next month, Maya is participating in the Regional Youth Swimming Championship. If she wins her 100-meter freestyle race, she will qualify for the National Games. Maya knows that if she stays focused and listens to her coach's advice, she will have a great chance of achieving her dream.

bai_doc.chu:
Maya is an eleven-year-old swimmer who trains at the National Junior Sports Academy. Every morning, Maya wakes up at 5:30 a.m. to prepare for her first training session. Being an elite athlete requires intense dedication, hard work, and strict discipline.
"If you want to reach the finals, you must practice every day," explains Coach Harrison. "If a swimmer skips training without a valid reason, they will lose their endurance very quickly."
At the academy, young athletes learn that success is not just about winning medals; it is also about staying healthy and respecting the rules of sportsmanship. Athletes need to follow a balanced diet rich in carbohydrates and protein. They ought to sleep at least nine hours every night so their muscles can recover properly. Coach Harrison always reminds his team: "You shouldn't eat junk food before a big race, and you mustn't forget to stretch your muscles before entering the pool. Skipping your warmup can cause severe muscle injuries."
However, training isn't always intense. On Sundays, Maya needn't wake up early because it is her official rest day. "Rest is just as important as hard work," Maya says. "If I take time to rest on Sunday, I will feel energized and ready for Monday's workouts."
Next month, Maya is participating in the Regional Youth Swimming Championship. If she wins her 100-meter freestyle race, she will qualify for the National Games. Maya knows that if she stays focused and listens to her coach's advice, she will have a great chance of achieving her dream.

bai_doc.chu:
Danny and his dad came to every city home game. And Danny acted as commentator because, when he was younger, his dad had been blinded in an accident. He’d had to stop work, stop playing football with Danny, stop almost everything.
Danny remembered worrying if his dad would give up going to the football too, but on the day of the first game, after he was out of hospital, dad had stood up.
‘Danny?’
‘Yeah.’
‘Come on, son. City are at home. What are you waiting for?’
Since then, Danny had become skilled at describing live football, telling his dad just enough so that he could follow the game…
…  The second half was fantastic. City poured players forward. Their twin strike force looked lethal. Sam Roberts, England’s leading scorer and new sensation, Ghanaian international Anthony Owusu. Danny struggled to keep up his commentary just as much as the United defenders struggled to keep up with City’s strikers.
‘Owusu is playing deep,’ Danny told his dad. ‘Roberts further up.’
And as he spoke, City’s midfield dynamo launched a high cross into the United area. The ball ricocheted off a defender to Owusu, who controlled it on his knee and volleyed it with amazing power. At first the ball seemed to be going well over, but then it began to dip into a powerful arc. Half a second later, it was crashing in off the crowbar and bouncing about in the goal.
One-nil. An awesome strike.
Danny and his dad leapt into each other’s arms as the crowd exploded. First with the loudest cheer of the season, then with the name of the scorer. Over and over again.
Ow-usu! Ow-usu! Ow-usu!
When the fans had gone quiet enough for anyone to talk, Dad spoke.
‘What happened?’
This always amused Danny. His dad would be leaping around, punching the air, screaming at the top of his voice one minute, then calmly asking to know why he’s been jumping around in the first place.
‘Owusu…’ Danny said breathlessly.
‘I gathered that.’
‘… he just blasted it in!’
‘Yeah?’
Danny knew his dad needed more. So he decided to give it to him: like a proper reporter on the radio. He breathed in and began.
‘City’s amazing Ghanaian international has scored the goal of the season. Picking the ball up on the edge of the area, he took it on his knee, then fired an unstoppable volley past the paralysed United keeper. That’s Owusu’s twentieth goal of the season. And just goes to show that he deserved the African Player of the Year award he received only two weeks ago.’

bai_doc.chu:
In December 1891, a gym teacher named James Naismith wanted to find a game his students could play indoors during the cold winters in Massachusetts. He nailed two peach baskets to the balcony railings of the gym and used a soccer ball for the game. Unlike today, the baskets had solid bottoms, so every time a player scored, the referee had to climb a ladder to get the ball back!
As the game grew, people made changes to make it faster and more exciting. In the beginning, there were no backboards, which meant fans in the balcony could reach over and block the shots. Backboards were added to stop this from happening. The soccer ball was eventually replaced by a larger orange ball that was easier to bounce and grip.
In 1946, the Basketball Association of America was formed, which later became the National Basketball Association (NBA) in 1949. This organization helped turn basketball into a professional sport. Today, players like LeBron James and Michael Jordan are famous for their skills, but it all began with a soccer ball and two peach baskets.

bai_doc.tieu_de: The Path of a Young Champion
bai_doc.tieu_de_html: The Path of a Young Champion
bai_doc.chu:
Maya is an eleven-year-old swimmer who trains at the National Junior Sports Academy. Every morning, Maya wakes up at 5:30 a.m. to prepare for her first training session. Being an elite athlete requires intense dedication, hard work, and strict discipline.
"If you want to reach the finals, you must practice every day," explains Coach Harrison. "If a swimmer skips training without a valid reason, they will lose their endurance very quickly."
At the academy, young athletes learn that success is not just about winning medals; it is also about staying healthy and respecting the rules of sportsmanship. Athletes need to follow a balanced diet rich in carbohydrates and protein. They ought to sleep at least nine hours every night so their muscles can recover properly. Coach Harrison always reminds his team: "You shouldn't eat junk food before a big race, and you mustn't forget to stretch your muscles before entering the pool. Skipping your warmup can cause severe muscle injuries."
However, training isn't always intense. On Sundays, Maya needn't wake up early because it is her official rest day. "Rest is just as important as hard work," Maya says. "If I take time to rest on Sunday, I will feel energized and ready for Monday's workouts."
Next month, Maya is participating in the Regional Youth Swimming Championship. If she wins her 100-meter freestyle race, she will qualify for the National Games. Maya knows that if she stays focused and listens to her coach's advice, she will have a great chance of achieving her dream.

dong: Nadine — I love playing volleyball because it’s easy to learn and great fun! All you need is a volleyball and a net. It’s played by two six-player teams on a court or on the beach. If they miss the ball or it hits the net, your opponent wins a point.

manh.html: The Ocean Food Chain Do you know what eats what in the ocean? Well, as with any food chain, the Marine Food Chain begins with plants
produce their own food using energy from the sun. A common sea plant is plankton
provides vitamins, proteins and minerals for primary consumers to feed on in the next link. This group is made up of small fish
float in the sea. Jellyfish and starfish are examples of these. Secondary consumers are common fish like minnows
eat the floating ones. Finally, there are the tertiary consumers
huge appetite means they eat all the smaller fish. They are usually large fish such as tuna or small sharks. It’s a fish-eat-fish world!

bai_doc.chu:
**1** The Dyeing Poison Dart Frog lives in tropical rainforests in dense foliage under leaves. It likes to stay close to the ground, although it has strong limbs which it can use to climb trees.

**2** It has brightly coloured skin with yellow on its back and blue on its legs. It is one of the largest species of poisonous frogs.

**3** Curiously, unlike most frogs that are nocturnal, poison dart frogs are more sociable during the day.

**4** It has just one natural predator ‘a snake’ which is immune to its poison.

**5** It is extremely toxic. Indigenous groups in the Amazon used its poison on the tips of their darts and arrows for hunting animals and defending themselves. That’s how it got its name!

It likes to stay close to the ground, although it has strong limbs which it can use to climb trees. 2 It has brightly coloured skin with yellow on its back and blue on its legs. It is one of the largest species of poisonous frogs. 3 Curiously, unlike most frogs that are nocturnal, poison dart frogs are more sociable during the day. 4 It has just one natural predator ‘a snake’ which is immune to its poison. 5 It is extremely toxic. Indigenous groups in the Amazon used its poison on the tips of their darts and arrows for hunting animals and defending themselves. That’s how it got its name!

bai_doc.tieu_de: Song for a Whale by Lynne Kelly
bai_doc.tieu_de_html: Song for a Whale by Lynne Kelly
bai_doc.chu:
The narrator of the story is a young girl called Iris, who is deaf. In this extract, Iris is in class with her interpreter, Mr. Charles, who uses sign language to help her understand her teacher, Ms. Amarillo.

The video started out with a whale swimming in the ocean. Because of the captions, I could read the words on the screen instead of from Mr. Charles’s hands. The dark gray-blue body of the whale filled up the screen, his tail waving up and down.

The narrator in the video talked about a whale called Blue 55, who swam around by himself and not in a pod, like other whales. As far as anyone knew, it had always been that way; he didn’t have any friends or a family to swim with or talk to. He was a type of baleen whale – the type that ate plankton and small fish, not the kind with teeth that ate squid and seals. But he was a hybrid. His mother was a blue whale, and his father a fin whale.

“The problem,” said the narrator, “is Blue 55’s unique voice. Most whales call out at frequencies of thirty-five hertz and lower, while this lonely whale’s sounds are at around fifty-five hertz.”

Only around 20 hertz off, but it made a big difference. He was speaking a language that only he knew.

“Furthermore, his song is in a unique pattern; even if the other whales can hear him, they don’t understand what he is saying. Blue 55 probably can’t communicate with his own parents.”

My stomach tightened into a ball. I wanted another whale on the screen to swim up to Blue 55, or at least look at him.

“The strange calls of Blue 55 were first detected by naval sonar in the late 1980s. Marine biologists figured out what was making the sounds and why the whale was all alone in the ocean.”

I didn’t notice until the words on the screen blurred that my eyes were watery. Mr. Charles handed me a tissue from his pocket. Maybe I’d sniffled or something.

“Allergies,” I signed, without looking away from the video.

The narrator went on to say that researchers from a marine sanctuary had tried to put a tracker on Blue 55, so they could follow his migration pattern, which was also weird and unlike other whales’. They got a sample of his skin to test. That was how they figured out his parents had been different species. But, before they could attach the tracker to him, Blue 55 dove down and swam away. He wouldn’t need to resurface for a breath for another twenty minutes. Without a tracker on him, the only way anyone ever knew where he was swimming was from underwater microphones that picked up his song.

I didn’t remember standing up, but when the video ended and Ms. Alamilla started talking, I had to look down to see Mr. Charles. Everyone’s eyes were on me as I slid back down into my chair. My textbook was on the floor – I must have knocked it off my desk when I stood up. I left it at my feet.

“Can you imagine that?” Ms. Alamilla asked. “Swimming around for all those years, unable to communicate with anyone?”

Yes.

She said something else about frequencies, but I wasn’t paying attention anymore. I looked through Mr. Charles, as if I could still see that whale on the screen.

Blue 55 didn’t have a pod of friends or a family who spoke his language. But he still sang. He was calling and calling, but no one heard him.

bai_doc.tieu_de: A morning with the bird survey team
bai_doc.tieu_de_html: A morning with the bird survey team
bai_doc.chu:
by young nature volunteer, Ella Tran

Last autumn, I joined a group of volunteers counting birds at a wetland reserve. We met just after sunrise. I expected to spend the whole morning beside the large lake, but our guide led us along a narrow path to several quiet pools instead. She explained that birds often feed there before visitors arrive.

At the first pool, I heard a strange whistling call. I searched the trees but could not see the bird. Finally, another volunteer pointed to a small kingfisher sitting on a low branch. Its blue-green feathers looked almost the same colour as the leaves in the early morning light.

Later, I noticed a large shape standing among the reeds. I thought it was a piece of wood until it moved its head. It was a heron, waiting silently for fish. I wanted to walk closer, but our guide reminded us that we should observe wildlife without disturbing it. We used binoculars instead.

The most exciting moment came when we spotted several young ducks following their mother through the water. I had seen ducks many times before, but I had never noticed how quickly the ducklings could change direction together.

Before leaving, we recorded the number of birds we had seen and compared our notes. Our guide explained that regular surveys help scientists notice changes in bird populations. My feet were wet and I was tired, but I was already looking forward to joining another survey.

bai_doc.chu:
written by Lucas Pham, Year 5 beach-watch volunteer

Last summer, I spent a Saturday helping a marine scientist called Dr Ross at a rocky beach. Our job was to find out which creatures lived in the rock pools. I thought we would need to swim, but Dr Ross explained that we only had to wait for the tide to go out.

When the water moved back, small pools appeared between the rocks. At first, they looked empty. Then I sat still for a few minutes, and a tiny crab came out from under a stone. Dr Ross said that many animals hide during the day to stay safe from gulls.

In the next pool, I found something that looked like a red flower. I reached out to touch it, but Dr Ross stopped me. It was a sea anemone, and its soft arms can sting small fish. She told us to look with our eyes and to use our hands only when she said it was safe.

The best part of the day came when my friend Hana found a starfish. It was bright orange and much bigger than my hand. Dr Ross showed us where it had lost one arm and was slowly growing a new one. I could hardly believe it!

At the end of the afternoon, we wrote down every creature we had seen and took photos of each pool. Dr Ross said that this information would show whether the beach was getting cleaner or dirtier over the years. My clothes were covered in sand and I was very hungry, but I felt proud that I had helped real scientists.

bai_doc.chu:
written by Mai Nguyen, member of the school nature club

In March, my older cousin invited me to join a mangrove planting day near the coast. I had never seen a mangrove tree before, so I imagined something like the tall trees in our local park. When we arrived, I was surprised to see short, twisted trees standing in muddy water.

Our leader, Mr Binh, gave each of us a bag of young plants. He showed us how to push them into the soft mud and press it firmly around the roots. It looked easy, but my boots kept getting stuck. Twice I almost fell over, and everyone laughed, including me.

While we worked, Mr Binh explained why mangroves are so important. Their roots hold the mud together, so the land is not washed away by big waves. Many young fish and crabs also shelter between the roots until they are big enough to live in the open sea.

Around midday, I noticed tiny holes all over the mud. Suddenly, dozens of small crabs ran out and waved one large claw in the air. Mr Binh told us they were fiddler crabs and that the males wave their claws to attract a mate. I watched them for so long that I forgot to eat my lunch.

By the afternoon, our group had planted more than two hundred young trees. Mr Binh said that only some of them would survive the first year, so volunteers would come back to check on them. I was covered in mud from head to toe, but on the way home I asked my cousin if I could join again next time.
